5 WAYS CHINET PAPER SERVICE 

can save time T money and worries in 
summer camp food service operations 

1. Cut Dishwashing Expense. 

Eliminate the initial replacement of maintenance cost of expensive dishwashing equipment that 
may only be used a few months out of the year. 

2. Cut the Spread of Germs. 

There is no germ problem with CHINET paper plates — they're sterilized when manufactured 
so they're hospital-clean when they're used. 

3. Eliminate Breakage And The Replacement Cost of China. 

Save the time, trouble and expense of buying matching tableware to replace plates, platters 
and bowls that crack, break or chip. 

4. Eliminate Clatter And Crash. 

Paper Service is quiet, make a meal more relaxing. 

5. Cut Waste Through Better Portion Control. 

CHINET plates come in all sizes, in both regular and compartment designs to make portion con¬ 
trol easier.

A Letter from the President 

Let me start off by saying that I 
hope everyone had a very success¬ 
ful, enjoyable and accident free 
summer. Your executive is now 
able to start working more earn¬ 
estly on future plans for C.C.A. and 
from what I can see, it appears that 
we will have a most exciting and 
interesting year. 

In consultation with our repre¬ 
sentative with the Fitness and Ama¬ 
teur Sport Department in Ottawa, 
we have been advised that we can 
go ahead and proceed with plans 
for the National Standards Work¬ 
shop next January. For those of 
you who were at the Halifax Con¬ 
ference, you will recall that this 
was a resolution and I am pleased 
that we will be able to act on this 
recommendation. It is anticipated 
that the workshop will be held 
January 20-23 in BanfF, and this 
will tie in with the annual meeting 
and conference of the Alberta 
Camping Association. Provincial 
Associations can now start making 
tentative plans for two representa¬ 
tives to attend this meeting — per¬ 


haps your President and Standards 
Chairman. 

I am sure that on July 22nd 
Doug Dent of Victoria, who was 
chairman of the National Camping 
Day breathed a sigh of relief. Our 
thanks to Doug for providing the 
leadership for this event. This is 
an endeavour which is extremely 
difficult to organize and I know 
that any suggestions you have as to 
how we can get this thing started 
earlier for next year, will certainly 
be appreciated. 

Claude Cousineau of the Uni¬ 
versity of Ottawa has agreed to 
chair a National Canoe School 
committee and he will soon be 
commencing plans for the estab¬ 
lishment of more Canoeing Schools 
for experienced canoeists not only 
lor next spring but for future years 
as well. 

As many of you know, the con¬ 
stitution of C.C.A. has many in¬ 
adequacies and in order to establish 
fully understood “ground rules", 
your executive formed a constitu¬ 
tional Task Force. This group met 
last spring and made several de¬ 
tailed recommendations for a re¬ 


vised constitution. These revisions 
were then sent on to each Provin¬ 
cial President. The task force will 
meet once again, this time in Van¬ 
couver on November 11, 12 and 13 
to study the proposals from the 
provincial associations. Following 
this, the second set of revisions will 
be sent to the provinces so that we 
can eventually gain ratification. 

Ann Prewitt, the publisher of 
our magazine recently had a very 
successful visit to the western prov¬ 
inces and was able to meet and 
consult with camping people in 
that region of the country. I am 
sure that Ann was able to pick up 
many new ideas and suggestions so 
that we can continue to provide a 
magazine which will be truly na¬ 
tional in interest and coverage. 

I hope that every member of 
C.C.A. will now make a note of the 
dates of the Board and Annual 
Meeting. These will be held in 
Montreal in conjunction with the 
Quebec Camping Association Con¬ 
ference and the dates will be April 
IS, 19, and 20. 

The news from Manitoba should 
be of interest to every province. 
Julian Smith, one of North Amer¬ 
ica’s leading experts in the field of 
outdoor education will be the guest 
speaker at the M.C.A. outdoor edu¬ 
cation conference. I am sure that it 
will be a most successful and stim¬ 
ulating conference. 

Speaking of information, I do 
hope that if any of you have any 
news, you will keep the National 
Office advised. And also I know 
that each provincial association 
would be very grateful for minutes 
of meetings and newsletters from 
every other provincial group. In 
other words, let’s keep one another 
informed as to what’s happening 
throughout Canada in camping. 
John Latimer 
President 

Canadian Camping 
Association 

It was with deep regret that 1 
heard of the death of Eric Russell 
of St. John's , Newfoundland. Eric 
was taken from us much too early 
in his life. He had been an active 
worker in Nexcfoundland for the 
Boy Scout's Association and was 
responsible for founding the New¬ 
foundland and Labrador Camping 
Association and was its president 
when the association became a 
member of C.C.A. 

Our sympathies are extended to 
Eric's wife and child.

The Canadian Camping Association’s Canoeing 

Instructors School 


by Andrea Dillon 
Department of Recreology 
University of Ottawa 


In the month of June candidates 
arrived from all over Canada to 
begin a very intensive eight day 
course which would hopefully lead 
to their being awarded the C.C.A.’s 
(Canadian Camping Association), 
Canoeing Instructors Certificate. 
The candidates on the course were 
presented with a new look and 
approach to canoeing. The canoe 
was the means of transportation 
that first opened Canada’s interior 
and now is sought as an opportun¬ 
ity to rediscover some of Canada’s 
heritage or simply as a way to enjoy 
the natural surroundings. As the 
canoe played such an important 
role in Canada's history the candi¬ 
date learned about the makes of 
canoes, the influence of geography 
on the style of these canoes as well 
as the human element attached to 
the evolution of the canoe. Perhaps 
what is more important the student 
learned how to apply this material, 
this knowledge, in his particular 
situation. 

The Canoeing Instructor’s School 
was first started in 1967 with a 
small group of enthusiastic canoe¬ 
ists under the direction and gui¬ 
dance of Claude Cousineau and 
Professor Kirk Wipper. The canoe 
school has just finished its fifth 
year of operation and has changed 
and expanded throughout these 
years. Originally the school offered 
one eight day course to both En¬ 
glish and French speaking men and 
women. After four years, the direc¬ 
tor decided to split the course and 
offer two eight day sessions. The 
increased interest and the fact that 
much of the course’s time was taken 
up in translating material due to 
the two languages proved the 



Students learn how to conduct fun games in a canoe. 
Here they are playing Canoe Basketball. 



The staff of the 1971 Canoeing Instructor's School, 
French Section. Left to right are: Claude Cousineau, 
Daniel Gauverneau, Suzanne St. Pierre, Kirk Wipper, 
Susan Cousineau, J. P. Faubert, and Gerry Gassett. 


5 






Claude Cousineau, one of the Directors of the C.C.A. 
Canoe Instructor's School. 



Part of the candidate's time is spent studying rapids 
and learning the intricacies of shooting them. 



change necessary. Both courses 
draw candidates from different 
areas of Canada adding a new 
dimension to the course as each 
student brings with him a different 
approach because of his particular 
situation. Though the students for 
the most part are actively involved 
in summer camp programs, many 
come from other working situa¬ 
tions. 

Presently the course is being di¬ 
rected towards canoeists with a 
fairly high level of skill. Students 
attending are expected to have a 
sound knowledge of canoe strokes 
and be familiar with the use of a 
canoe. This basic requirement al¬ 
lows for more course time to be 
spent on teaching techniques, 
learning patterns, tripping skills, 
and organizational methods. In its 
formative years the school catered 
to providing a canoe instructor 
skilled in the techniques of strokes 
and dock teaching. Today many 
canoe programs are now increasing 
the performance of tripping within 
the individual canoe programs. 
Realizing this trend the course of¬ 
fers the candidates a good orienta¬ 
tion for conducting such a pro¬ 
gram. Students receive theory and 
practical sessions on tripping pro¬ 
grams; how to organize such a pro¬ 
gram from the outset, budgeting 
for equipment, food, pre-trip train¬ 
ing programs, and learning meth¬ 
ods of how to make such a trip a 
real learning and living experience 
for all involved. The students take 
a two day canoe trip within their 
eight day session which gives them 
the opportunity to experiment 
with techniques and methods in¬ 
troduced earlier in the course. This 
short trip also provides the candi¬ 
dates with the chance to exchange 
some of their own tricks that they 
may have found useful from pre¬ 
vious experience. 

As a former student describing 
the course, one point that cannot 
be overlooked is that of the inter¬ 
action between attending students. 
Each of the candidates brings with 
them experiences and knowledge 
of programs existing in their spe¬ 
cific area. The course provides the 
opportunity for these people to 
discuss the differences and compare. 
Perhaps the overriding theme that 
the student takes away with him is 
that the canoe instructor of today 
is not limited within his canoeing 
program, rather the program can 
offer a limitless view into conserva¬ 
tion, ecology, outdoor education, to 
name a few, through the working 
use of the canoe.

par Susan Cousineau 

Thirty-jour new canoeing 
instructors 

The Canadian Camping Asso¬ 
ciation offered again this year the 
Annual Canoeing Instructors 
School held at the University of Ot¬ 
tawa Camp, Gracefield, Quebec. For 
the second year the School received 
a grant from the Fitness & Amateur 
Sport Division of the National 
Health & Welfare Ministry. This 
financial aid helped cover part of 
the travelling expenses of candi¬ 
dates residing outside of Quebec 
and Ontario. It also permitted to 
reduce the tuition fees of each can¬ 
didate to a bare minimum of $30.00 
for the 8 day duration. The admin¬ 


istration of the school was handled 
by the Department of Recreology 
of the University of Ottawa. 

The School was offered in two 
parts — the French School — June 
8-15 and the English School — June 
16-24 th. Under the leadership of 
Director Claude Cousineau and 
guest professor Kirk Wipper, sev¬ 
enty candidates from almost every 
province in Canada participated. 
Gerry Fassett, Daniel Gauvreau, 
Rejean Vachon, Jean-Pierre Fau¬ 
bert, Howard Rosenthal, Doug 
Wipper, Suzanne St-Pierre, Susan 
Cousineau and Andrea Dillon were 
the Instructors teaching for the 
Schools. 

The intensive program of each 
School was highlighted this year by 
a three-day canoe trip and the use 
of a video-tape machine. Such ac¬ 
tivities as shooting rapids, canoe 
games, slalom courses along with 
the theoretical side of canoeing 
were also included. 

Congratulations to all the 
successful candidates. Among the 
participants, 34 received the men¬ 
tion “Instructor”. They are the 
following: 

Lucie Beauchesne, Louis Begin, 
Caroline Boucher, Paul Calve, 
Gerard Champigny, Nicole Gali¬ 
peau, Claude Hebert, Christine 
Kemper, Claude Langelier, Nor¬ 
mand Lapierre, Gaston Lemire, 
Bruno Poirier, Leo Robitaille, 
Claude St-Louis, Alan Bocking, 
Peter Callandine, Ted Cohen, Rob¬ 
ert Dawson, Tom Duck, Roy Funk, 
Mary Garland, Jeffrey Hackler, 
Robert Lamberton, Sandy McClel¬ 
land, Garth McKane, Seil Mens, 
Filberto Montis, Donald Pentz, 
John Rodger, Jocelyn Schaffens¬ 
burg, Catherine Smith, Don Wad¬ 
dell, Hubie Weller, Linda Brain.

Relations Moniteurs Campeurs 

par Bruno Roy 
Camp St-arsene 


Acceptant qu'une notion totali- 
taire de l’cducation est moins pro- 
bable de nos jours, le moniteur se 
definit connne un entraineur, un 
eveilleur d’hommes. Non un ora- 
teur ou un adjudant. II est le 
compagnon de vie de l’enfant en 
vacances, celui qui precisement 
1 emplace les parents sur le triple 
plan materiel, moral et spirituel. II 
est la presence adulte aupres du 
campeur. Force est d’avouer l’im- 
portance de ses relations avec les 
jeunes de sa colonie. 

C’est un lieu comrnun de dire 
que c’est dans la valeur relation- 
nelle des personnes que le moniteur 
se doit d’exceller. Mais qu’est-ce 
done, d’abord, une relation hu- 
maine? C’est un processus d’inter- 
action qui creee autour d’un indi- 
vidu ou d’un groupe des liens phy¬ 
siques, affectifs et sociaux par un 
procede de communication et de 
participation qui conduit cet indi- 
vidu ou ce groupe a un apprentis- 
sage a l'autonomie, e’est-a-dire du 
respect de la liber te d’autrui et du 
bon emploi de la sienne. Trois 
sortes de “leadership” se presentent 
pour repondre aux objectifs des 
relations humaines: 1’autocratie, 
l’anarchie (ou le laisser-faire) et la 
democratic. Ces trois types de re¬ 
lations commendent des techniques 
d’action, des implications et des 
consequences differentes. Le moni¬ 
teur doit en etre conscient. 


Relations du ?nonitcur avec 
son groupe 

L’autocratic. Ce type de relations 
fait appel a des regies fixes, a un 
controle regulier et strict. Les de¬ 
cisions, bien qu’arbitraires, appar- 
tiennent au chef. Tout est domina¬ 
tion et dirigisme. Le dialogue et la 
liber te sont ignores. Tout est “se- 
curisation” pour une apparente 
harmonie. L’attitude des campeurs, 
cependant, sera une sorte de resig¬ 
nation plus ou moins consciente 
manifestee par tine soumission col¬ 
lective. Ce groupe autocratique 
(etat de dependance par rapport 
au chef) n’aura aticune prise de 
conscience personnclle. Sur le plan 
individuel, le campeur se refermera 
sur lui-meme. 

L* anarchic. L’autorite n’existe 
pas. C’est un laisser-faire qui 
n’exige aucune regie precise, qui ne 
souffle d’aucun controle. L’auto- 
rite ne pent intervenir et si elle 
cxiste elle sera demolie avec les 
structures qui la supporte. Les rela¬ 
tions ont l’avantage d’etre natu- 
relles. Par contre, c’est le regne de 
la “loi du plus fort”. Les plus 
faibles sont negliges. Car dans tout 
groupe anarchique, le plus fort 
obtient ce qu’il vent. C’est la dicta- 
ture du “leader” improvise. Au 
plan collectif, l’insolement (la 
bande) caracterisera un climat d’in- 
securite. L’individualisme lese ainsi 
les valeurs sociales primordiales a 
cet age de la vie. Le campeur se 
restreint dans un egoisme nefaste. 
II peut aussi developper un sens de 
l’adaptation qui favorisera son sens 


createur. Mais ce n’est pas toujours 
le cas, malheureusement, pour les 
campeurs plus faibles et dclaisses. 

Im democratic, Elle favorise la 
participation collective aux deci¬ 
sions. Le dialogue est en vigueur. 
Les suggestions sont les bienvenues. 
L’exemple du moniteur devient im¬ 
portant. II agit indirectement et 
favorise le partage des responsa- 
bilitcs. Tout devient coordination 
et souplesse. Le campeur ne refute 
pas s’il est concerte sur le bon 
fonctionnement du groupe; il ad¬ 
here dans toute sa spontaneite. Le 
moniteur dans le partage de ses 
pouvoirs assure ainsi une securite 
psychologique au groupe dont il 
devient indiscutablement le respon- 
sable desire et accepte. 

D’aucuns diront, premierement, 
cjue la superioritc naturelle que le 
moniteur deploie sur ses campeurs 
risque d’entravel* la valeur humaine 
de ses relations en glissant sur la 
pente facile du commendement qui 
reclamme une obeissance passive et 
cjue, deuxiemement, la fonction 
corrective de la discipline con tied it 
toute education a la liberte et au 
dialogue. Jc pense, a ce propos, que 
la discipline est avant tout une 
attitude de cooperation. Cette atti¬ 
tude elimine le pesant probleme de 
1’autorite et nous fait user de nos 
pouvoirs avec economie. Car moins 
on a d’autoritc reelle plus les 
marques exterieures se font ijnpor¬ 
ta ntes et repetees. Le moniteur doit 
etre capable de prevention, d’or- 

Co ntinued on page 18

Camper-Counsellor Relations 

by Bruno Roy 
Camp St-arsene 


Nowadays, with the unlikely fact 
of a universal idea of education, the 
counsellor is defined as a trainer, a 
mind awakener, not a speaker or an 
adjutant. He is the life companion 
ol the child on vacation, the one 
who replaces the parents in three 
aspects: material, moral and spirit¬ 
ual. He is the adult presence to the 
camper. We have to recognize the 
importance of his relations with the 
youth of his group. 

It is commonly said that the 
counsellor has to excel in the value 
of personal relationships. But, first 
of all, what is a human relation? It 
is an interacting process which 
creates physical, affective and social 
ties around an individual or a 
group, by way of communication 
and participation, conducting this 
individual or group to an appren¬ 
ticeship in autonomy, that is to say, 
of the respect for others’ liberties 
and the good use of his own. There 
are three kinds of leadership that 
lead to human relations’ objectives: 
Autocracy, Anarchy (or, “let things 
take their course’’) and Democracy. 
These three types of relations de¬ 


mand different techniques of ac¬ 
tion, implications and consequen¬ 
ces. The counsellor has to be 
conscious of them. 

The Counsellor's Relations 
with his Group 

Autocracy. This type of relation 
asks for fixed rules and strict and 
regular control. Decisions, even if 
they are arbitrary, are left to the 
chief. Domination and command 
are everything. Dialogue and liber¬ 
ty are non-existent. It is “making 
everything secure” for an apparent 
harmony. Yet, the campers attitude 
will be more or less one of con¬ 
scious resignation, manifested by a 
collective obedience. This auto¬ 
cratic group (independent from 
the leader) will have no self aware¬ 
ness. On the individual plane, the 
camper will isolate himself from 
the others. 

Anarchy. Authority does not exist. 
It is a “let things take their course” 
(attitude) which does not demand 
particular rules nor suffers from 
controls. Authority cannot inter¬ 
fere and if it exists it will be over¬ 
thrown, along with its supporting 


structures. The relationships have 
the advantage of being natural, but 
it’s the “law of the jungle”. The 
weaker ones are neglected, while, 
like in all anarchial groups, the 
stronger ones obtain all they want. 
It is the dictatorship of the impro¬ 
vised leader. On the collective 
plane, isolation will create an at¬ 
mosphere of insecurity. Individual¬ 
ism, in this way, encroaches upon 
the social values which are so im¬ 
portant at that age. The camper 
retires into a baneful egotism. He 
can also develop a sense of adapta¬ 
tion that will be advantageous to 
his sense of creativity. But, unfor¬ 
tunately, for the weaker and ne¬ 
glected camper, it is not always the 
case. 

Democracy is favourable to collec¬ 
tive participation and decision 
making. Dialogue exists and sug¬ 
gestions are welcome. The counsel¬ 
lor’s example becomes important. 
He acts indirectly and favours 
sharing of responsibilities. Every¬ 
thing is coordinated and flexible. 
The camper will not controvert the 
operation of the camp if he is 
integrated in its administration; his 
cooperation will be spontaneous. 
By sharing his power, the counsel¬ 
lor assures a psychological security 
to the group for which he undoubt¬ 
edly becomes the desired and ac¬ 
cepted leader. 

Some will say that, primarily, the 
natural superiority of the counsel¬ 
lor can hinder the value of his 
human relations if he tends to seek 
a passive obedience, and secondly, 
that the corrective function of dis¬ 
cipline contradicts any education 
in freedom and dialogue. On this 
matter, I think that discipline is 
mainly achieved by cooperation. 
This attitude eliminates the weigh¬ 
ty problem of authority, and, 
consequently, makes us use our 
prerogatives sparingly. The less our 

Continued on page 79

Horses For Sale 

by Hank Roessingh 
Director, Silvercreek Ranch, Calgary 
National Standards Chairman, C.C.A. 


After twelve years of operating 
a camp with a horseback riding 
program as one of the main fea¬ 
tures, my wife and 1 have come to 
the firm conclusion that it isn’t 
worth it. If any of you, camp 
directors, don’t have horses at camp 
now and are considering to give in 
to pressure from horse-crazy camp- 
kids and start a riding program, 
take my advice: don’t do it. We are 
going to trade in our horses for 
canoes, flood part of our campsite, 
and have a waterfront program 
providing us with peace of mind 
and wealth. 

We have had all kinds of animals 
at our camp over the years; dogs, 
cats, lambs, pigs, rabbits, a chamel¬ 
eon, a falcon and even a pet moose 
calf; i’ll put up with any of them if 
that pleases the campers, but no 
more horses. 

It all starts in late winter, when 
you are trying to put a decent staff 
for the summer together. Just be¬ 
cause we were ill advised enough to 
call our camp a Ranch, we attract 
applications from youngsters all 
over the continent who claim to 


know at least what a horse looks 
like and have visions of playing 
cowboy all summer. Any counselers 
with skills like crafts, singing, camp- 
crafts, nature study and all those 
other things we like to do at camp, 
send their applications elsewhere. 

But the real misery comes with 
the horses themselves. Horses get 
sick from an unbelievable variety 
of diseases, horses are temperamen¬ 
tal, and when they are ponies they 
are often outright cantankerous, 
horses hide in the bush or crawl 
through the fence and run away 
when you need them most, from 
campsites on outtrips they run 
away even when hobbled, horses 
cause accidents, their front end 
bites and their rear end kicks, they 
step on your foot when you are 
saddling them, they spook when 
you least expect it, they forget 
everything you have taught them 
in months of training as soon as a 
camp kid gets on them, but remem¬ 
ber such stupid things as which side 
should be curried first and kick up 
a fuss when you reverse the se¬ 
quence. 


Compare that to canoes. After 
you are through canoeing, you 
either tie up the canoe or drag it on 
land and forget it; it will be there, 
ready to go when you need it again 
after a day or a week. Tie up a 
horse and come back after a week 
and it will have starved to death; 
leave it untied and come back after 
five minutes and it’s gone. When a 
canoe gets damaged, you fix it and 
that is it; when a horse gets dis¬ 
temper, you have to call the vet and 
get all your horses inoculated at 
great expense. When the summer 
is over, you can put your canoes 
away, come back in spring to give 
them a coat of paint, and they’ll be 
ready to go next summer. But 
horses . . . ? They have to be fed, 
they have to be checked, they have 
to be rounded up when they get out 
of the fence, they have to be pam¬ 
pered when they foal; horses are an 
all-year worry and an all-year ex¬ 
pense. 

We have had all kinds of horses 
at our camp: big ones and little 
ones, gentle ones and wild ones, 
colts and old nags, horses that 
wouldn’t go and horses that 
wouldn't stop, horses that buck and 
horses that roll, and even some 
horses that we really liked; but 
across the board, once again: don’t 
start it. This summer we had a 
pinto pony who was very popular 
with the kids, so he got a lot of 
work to do. He became very smart 
at hiding in the bush when we 
rounded up the horses in the morn¬ 
ing. So we tied a bell around his 
neck. So he would stand still when 
he heard us coming, and we still 
couldn’t find him. But as soon as 
the day’s program was over and the 
dinnerbell rang, he woidd come out 
of hiding and demand his oats. 
Most horses are almost impossible 
to catch. When you approach them 
with a bucket of oats, they know 
when you have a rope or even a 
piece of baling string behind your 
back and they won’t come anywhere 
near you. Other horses have such 
idiosyncrasies as not wanting to be 
saddled in a stall or not wanting to 
be mounted in the barnyard. Un¬ 
less you know the individual likes 



Making friends with one of the ponies. 


10 


and dislikes of every one of your 
horses, you are asking for trouble 
when turning the campers loose on 
them. 

The worst time of all is when 
you have to buy horses. Horse sel¬ 
lers have as many ways to camou¬ 
flage the defects of their horses as 
the horses have defects. So at the 
horse sale, all horses appear to be 
sound, gentle and well trained. No 
seller will ever admit to selling a 
horse more than eight years old. 
One exceptionally honest seller said 
of his mare he wanted to sell, that 
he didn’t know how old she was. 
What he did know and didn’t tell, 
was that his grandfather owned the 
horse 25 years ago. At the horse sale 
there are horses who have spent all 
their lives on the prairies and have 
never seen a tree. Take them to the 
forests of the foothills, and they’ll 
walk under branches that scrape the 
kids off their backs, or walk be¬ 
tween trees leaving only one inch 
on each side, and break both knees 
of the rider all at once. 

All right, so you don’t buy horses 
with unknown pasts at the sale. So 
you buy horses from your neigh¬ 
bours who have received so much 
hospitality at your camp and who 
surely want to do business with you 
again in the future. Except that for 
them, there is a year-around open 
season on city slickers, and getting 
a few dollars out of a city man to 
them is not cheating, that is just 
having some fun. So you’ll find that 
suddenly you don’t really own the 
horse that you thought you just 
bought, or that the pony with all 
the virtues that the farmgirl reluc¬ 
tantly sold because she now had a 
bigger horse, is really so spoiled 
that it won’t even graze and will 
starve unless hand-fed, and that the 
good looking three-year-old that 
you bought for such a good price, 
was recently stolen from your camp 
cook. No, give me canoes any time. 
You go to your tried and tested 
dealer and you are assured of the 
same quality as you got last time 
around. No hidden defects, no 
doubts about the price and quality; 
a nice straightforward deal. 

I know, some of the camp kids 
will be heart-broken when there are 
no horses at camp. But I won’t have 
to answer questions about their 
favorites any more: “Is Rusty at 
camp this summer?”, “How is 
Dixie’s colt doing?”, “Can I ride 
Popcorn this time?” etc. etc. A 
canoe is a canoe; no favorites, just 
stick the kids in and shove them 
off. What a relief. 

Anybody want to buy my horses? 
Or trade them for canoes? 



Little Deer River. 



It takes time to get the horses saddled and the kids mounted. 



Races are popular but the horses are fickle.

As Camp Closes 

by M. C. MacCulloch, Director , Bolton Summer Camp 

Rotary Division 


Dear Stan: 

By now you are deeply entombed 
in your “other” life back in the 
city. 

I have just returned from closing 
camp for another winter. It is quiet 
there now. As I walked down past 
your cabin and the others, the 
rustlings, scratchings and mur- 
mtilings announced the camp’s re¬ 
possession by squirrels, chipmunks, 
and field mice. A collective sigh of 
Nature’s relief seemed to waft 
through the trees and across the 
clearings. Raccoons, groundhogs 
and rabbits have taken up the busi¬ 
ness of living undisturbed and un¬ 
hampered by us, the aliens. 

As I watched the breeze lay those 
old elms bare, I recalled and 
brooded, tranquil in the fading 
sunlight. Hence this little note to 
you, Stan. 

Last summer was a delight for 
me. My fears and worries before 
June for a successful and a person¬ 
ally satisfying summer were quickly 
allayed. I am most grateful for your 
help this summer and compliment 
you on the fine job you did. It isn’t 
every day one meets people who 
transmit on the same wave length 
—I felt we all did. May your tribe 
increase! 

1 hope that you can find time this 
winter to share your reflections of 
the summer and your current ad¬ 
ventures with me. 

1 am harbouring your promise to 
return for another summer. I hope 
that you will not disappoint me. I 
have a bad heart, high blood pres¬ 
sure, and housemaid’s knee, so you 
will realize that time is of the 
essence. 


Life is too terribly short and as I 
grow older I tend to relish more 
deeply the sudden chance commu¬ 
nications with human beings who 
are not afraid to share the riches of 
their spirits with strangers at camp, 
all in the interest of its’ cause. 

*Gnothi seauton, 
Clare. 

*Know thyself. 

Dear Sir: 

I feel slightly awed — slightly 
proud — inwardly envious and out¬ 
wardly humbled when I think of 
your letter and the kind words you 
said to me as the bus pulled away 
from camp in August. Your friend¬ 
ly coercion is a subtle shoio of 
friendship and I appreciate it. 

I am midway into my first year 
at University and I am having the 
time of my life. As a matter of fact, 
my life is being altered as you 
warned me in the summer. I fear 
that the days of wine and roses, i.e. 
summers as a camp counsellor are 
no longer. I am afraid that they are 
gone, forever! 

You once read to us, “All is a 
tremendous responsibility here but 
also a tremendous opportunity for 
all of us, 

And so I believe in children, 

And so I believe in good camps. 

And so I believe in this camp 
and I know luhy? 

What do you believe in and 
why?” 

And you also read to us, 

“For me as for some of you peo¬ 
ple who also return here year after 
year, the ideal summer is to be a 
member of this staff, for the friends 
I have made, the memories I can 
share and the rich dividends in 
human relations which I have 
gained over the years. For those of 


you who are new I must warn you 
that there is a magic about this 
camp. It gets into your blood and 
once there you cannot get it out.” 

That last sentence is the rub, the 
climax, the major pomt of differ¬ 
ence! I have more friends; my 
shared memories are immortal and 
I am rich from the dividends in 
human relationships which I have 
gained. There is a magic about 
camp — but prolonged magic is 
unreal. I have given to camp arid I 
certainly have received from camp 
— but unlike you — to me, return¬ 
ing would only be a denouement. A 
denouement of memories . 

Camp is for the kids — and if I 
went back for the purpose of hav- 
ing a good time or recapturing 
memories rather than for the kids, 
I would be a hypocrite — hypo¬ 
critical to my principles! 

I do hope with deep and true 
sincerity that my decision to leave 
camp for the campers, tuill not in¬ 
fluence our friendship. 

Sincerely, 

Stan. 

Dear Stan: 

Well! 

I wish to point out to you some 
immediate thoughts, perhaps not 
as philosophically sound as they 
should be due to their instantan¬ 
eous nature for your digestion. 

1 believe that the opportunities 
at camp are unlimited. Camp 
doesn’t drain into your system any 
“X” amount of happiness, fulfil¬ 
ment, reward or experience and 
then stop, measuring your portion 
as complete. This is my fourteenth 
summer at camp, eleven years at 
“our” camp so it is obvious that 
camping is a part of my life — the 
way I am conditioned to spend my 
summers. 


12 


I don’t think we are discussing 
jobs any more. It matters not 
whether you have personally de¬ 
cided on another role for your 
summer job. We are into the phil¬ 
osophy of camping — a much more 
important field, and one whose 
arms are far reaching and can affect 
your whole being for years to come. 

I do not feel that the adult who 
goes to camp for the summer has 
the dream of a child or camper. 1 
can still feel wonder at the dew on 
a cobweb, or watching the spider 
spin his home and at awe with a 
God who builds the blind bird’s 
nest, or content with the personal 
satisfaction that I find and relish in 
good times, with good friends in a 
setting which pleases my spirit and 
eye. Is that who you mean? 

Only because 1 am older, and by 
no pretense wiser, do I say the 
following. 

Your mind I can see and under¬ 
stand has been liberated and the 
scope of reality now appears to be 
such a slender slice of life. Univer¬ 
sity is not high school. I remember. 
Your life must be compressed with 
new experiences, broadening ideas 
and a completely varied daily liv¬ 
ing, so sophisticated from our lives 
at camp. I beg you, bear caution. 
All is not new. 

Emotions do not change, only 
the method, and the setting of the 
telling varies. The theme is as con¬ 
stant as the northern star. Don’t ex¬ 
pect to find a new theme away from 
camp. 

The magic is not unrealistic of a 
repeated situation. God forbid that 
we should only live practical lives. 
That would even exclude laughter, 


tears, small talk after campers have 
gone to bed and even children. 
Everyone knows that children are 
more trouble than they are worth. 

No, the magic is not childlike. 
It is not prolonged for adults. 
Every new camper, every new coun¬ 
sellor, every new day starts it all 
over again. To see you must but 
open your eyes and look. I beg you 
to look. 

And why should camp be only 
for the campers? 

I am a normal adult with certain 
needs and these need fulfilment for 
me just as they do for the children. 
Gan we not find satisfaction in the 
same things but different means? 

My students ask me why we must 
study poetry. Does that mean I 
should stop? I shall read it, with 
the hope that some student will 
catch my interest, my love, my 
spirit, as I once did from an English 
teacher years ago. One child per 
summer makes it worthwhile and 
an excellent record. 

And let’s be practical. What 
other summer job can touch sitting 
at those lookouts, master of all you 
survey, Windy Top in the morning 
mist, or our Hill on a rainy week? 

O. Henry once said, “I’m a grown 
person with masculine proclivities 
and habits of self-defence, but there 
is a time when all systems of ego¬ 
tism and predominance fail.” I feel 
that way now with your decision to 
give up camping. 

This lecture finds me in good 
health and poor spirits but I shall 
rally in the hour. Do keep in touch. 

Gnothi Seauton, 
Clare. 


Dear Sir: 

I found your letter to be strik¬ 
ingly meaningful. I do apologize 
for the time lapse but I needed time 
to think. 

I find myself finally agreeing with 
your interpretation of camp life 
entirely. I feel that the materialistic 
and non materialistic splendors of 
camp are as dear to me now as they 
are to you. I learned at camp — and 
as you said, learning is life." Pro¬ 
longed magic is practical. 

I believe that kids should get out 
of the city and have a good time at 
camp. There is a song we sing 
around here which goes, “There 
but for fortune may go you or I, 
you or I” I am luckier than a lot of 
“our” kids — they deserve a holiday 
and they deserve good guidance. I 
now feel the urge, and the need to 
help them. Is that what you were 
trying to tell me camping is all 
about? 

I hope that my thoughts are co¬ 
herent. This has been an uncertain 
year for me. The newness of it has 
forced me to examine a lot of my 
ideas. Thank you for your help and 
your concern. Some day I am sure 
l will really appreciate your patient 
guidance. 

Yours very truly, 
Staii. 

P.S. Would you please send me an 
application form. You have a job I 
wish to apply for!

Unique Aspects of Waterfronts in Ocean 

Environments 

Tom Creighton, Director YMCA Big Cove Camp & Former President 

of N, S. Camping Association 


The cry of the sea gull, the smell 
of the salt air, the aroma of low tide 
on the beach, the sights and sounds 
of the surf, the beauty in the shape 
of the clam shell, and the sight of 
the yellow sea weed waving in the 
waves, — are all of these romantic? 
Oh, yes! Having lived on both sides 
of the country, the sea is in my 
being and no lake, however beauti¬ 
ful, can compare. The romantic in 
me loves the sea, but the practical 
camp director administering a facil¬ 
ity and a programme in a coastal 
camp says that the sea is a pain in 
the neck when running a camp. 
But 1 still do not say that the sea is 
not a place to have a camp. 

The two obvious factors that 
make an ocean environment differ¬ 
ent are those of tidal action and 
the chemistry of the sea and the 
action of the life within the sea. 
These factors affect not only pro¬ 
gramming, facility construction and 
maintenance, but also the types of 
facilities and equipment used. No 
one ocean location is typical as is 
no lake setting and therefore the 
conditions found in each camp are 
quite variable. 

Tide is a factor in the size of a 
waterfront facility in that a camp 
must have water for programme at 
all levels of tide. An effective water¬ 
front can only be constructed in a 
location where the tidal variation 
is not extreme. Camps located in 
the Bay of Fundy area of Nova 
Scotia must realistically develop 
swimming pools rather than utilize 
the ocean as the costs and difficul¬ 
ties of dealing with 24-foot tidal 
variations are staggering. A facility 
developed in tidal waters may only 
be one third usable at low tide and 
to overcome this a much longer 
dock than would be necessary in a 
lake needs to be constructed; the 
alternative being a program related 
to the times water levels are suit¬ 
able. As tides are variable in size 
and in time from day to day the 
scheduling becomes unrealistic. 

Other consideration with tide are 


the usability of the beach exposed 
at low tide. Shells (which are the 
bane of the band-aid dispensers), 
slippery rocks, and mud become 
exposed lessening the enjoyment by 
children and increasing the risks of 
accidents. Raking of the beach be¬ 
comes a regular maintenance chore. 
The tide will also fill up a beach 
with debris, or, in reverse, take 
away sand added by the camp to 
build up a good beach. 

Patterns of construction are dif¬ 
ferent depending on local condi¬ 
tions such as materials, ice develop¬ 
ment, capital, etc. In British Col¬ 
umbia a common style is a per¬ 
manent dock atop creosoted pilings 
reaching out beyond the tide line 
from which one proceeds down a 
ramp to a float where floating lines 
delineate the swimming areas. In 
the east, where ice conditions exist, 
two forms are common: rock filled 
cribs are extended out into the 
water to the low tide line leading 
to a ramp and float or a portable 
set of floating docks supported by 
styrofoam which must be removed 
in the fall. 

From a safety point of view tidal 
conditions force a camp to take 
more precautions as a greater area 
must be supervised. Areas that are 
clear of obstacles at high tide are 
hazards at low tide, and currents 
created by changing tides, especially 
in constricted waters, are dangers 
to swimmers and boaters. 

Most camps in the Maritimes are 
established away from coastal areas 
for a number of reasons. Climatic¬ 
ally the coast is cool and subject to 
more fog and inclement weather. 
Temperatures of the water except 
in inlet coves are too cold for swim¬ 
ming. Exposed shores are windy, 
cool and dangerous. Beaches are 
difficult to maintain or create. 

Maintenance problems for docks 
and boats are considerably in¬ 
creased with exposure to salt water 
and marine growth. Active growth 
of barnacles, algae, and boring an¬ 
imals makes maintenance a con¬ 


tinuous cycle of scraping, treating, 
and replacing. Treatment with a 
copper base paint will retard the 
action marine life causes. A piece 
of wood left in warm salt water 
will be reduced to a sponge-like 
consistency within a summer. These 
growths are also a hazard to chil¬ 
dren climbing on ladders and 
docks. Aluminum construction is 
impossible as electrolysis develops 
with the action of the salt water 
and the metal. 

Programming is affected by loca¬ 
tion in varying degrees. Children 
may have adjustment problems to 
the aesthetics of swimming in salt 
water — to its "salty” taste, to the 
dry sticky feeling after coming out 
of the water, or to the sting of the 
jelly fish. One summer when the 
presence of jellyfish, which are 
brought in by prevailing wind and 
current, were particularly virulent 
we had an alarming drop in swim¬ 
ming participation. Limitations are 
imposed on the effective use of 
canoes by consistently rough water 
conditions, lack of any volume of 
safe coastline, and the lack of ad¬ 
jacent inland water routes. From 
these points-of-view the sea coast 
environment is limiting. 

Pollution is as much a part of the 
seacoast environment as anywhere 
else. Pulp mills are located on sea 
coasts. Sewer systems have always 
found a place in the sea because 
man has often considered that the 
sea was a bottomless never-ending 
sewer. Our beautiful cove now has 
phosphate enriched eel grass grow¬ 
ing abundantly, its shell Fish are 
now condemned because of the 
effluent from nearby communities. 
Oil discharges from ships or the 
results of accidents to ships is an 
ever present hazard. 

From a positive viewpoint the 
ecology of the sea opens a new 
horizon for exploration and knowl¬ 
edge to be gained from this eco¬ 
system. Programmes in nature, 
crafts, exploration can capitalize 
on the environmental features.

The Canadian Camping Magazine and How 

We Came By It 

by Charles F. Plewman 


It was in the fall of 1944, a long 
and exhausting war was slowly 
drawing to a close. 

The “Originals”, the small group 
that had formed the Ontario 
Camping Association eleven years 
before and had nurtured it during 
its infancy, were still holding the 
fort. As one of the “old guard” who 
had still managed to evade office 
(I was secretary of the Toronto 
Red Cross and had Kilcoo Camp 
on my hands), I was literally 
drafted into the presidency. My job 
was to bridge the gap until the war 
was won and the new oncoming 
generation could take over. This 
then was to mark the end of the 
first epoch in the history of the On¬ 
tario Camping Association, Can¬ 
ada’s first organization of this kind. 
The “Originals” had traded offices, 
had shot their bolt and were now 
washed up. 

It was immediately evident to me 
that something was lacking. Ninety 
percent of all the camps in Ontario 
emanated from Toronto and all of 
the O.C.A. officers came from the 
same place. We were an Ontario 
Camping Association but in name 
only. Obviously something had to 
be done to interest and to involve 
Camp Directors who lived in other 
parts of the Province. 

The pressures of the war were 
such that annual Camp Confer¬ 
ences had gone by the board and 
were only held sporadically. The 
answer was clear, we needed a 
magazine or bulletin of some kind 


to draw us closer together. 

Armed with this conviction I 
approached the T. Eaton Company 
and asked them if they would fi¬ 
nance the first edition, which they 
did. 

As an association we were poor 
and just didn’t have the money. 
Next I asked the one and only 
Mary Edgar to act as Editor and 
she agreed. 

Before very long, I think it was 
in 1946, the Canadian Camping 
Association was formed at a meet¬ 
ing held in the Chateau Laurier in 
Ottawa. Jt grew out of the feeling 
that the time had come to have a 
national camping association and 
one that should stimulate the 
growth and development of camp¬ 
ing throughout the whole of Can¬ 
ada. While it was called the Can¬ 
adian Camping Association, in 
reality, nearly all of its members 
were representatives from the On¬ 
tario and Quebec Associations. To 
the best of my knowledge no other 
Province had a camping associa¬ 
tion. 

Just as in 1944 the O.C.A. had to 
widen out to represent and include 
the entire Province, so too the new 
and fragile Canadian Camping As¬ 
sociation had to take steps to make 
itself truly national; for the mo¬ 
ment it had no corporate existence. 

If after Confederation Canada 
needed the CPR to hold it together, 
so now the Canadian Camping 
Association needed something to 
make it a National reality. 

To the credit of the Ontario 
Camping Association, and its vision 
of the Canada of to-morrow, it 
closed out the Ontario Bulletin in 
1947 and threw its entire resources 
behind “Canadian Camping”, a 
mimeographed bulletin published 
quarterly and edited as before by 


Mary Edgar. Except for the change 
of the name, the format was the 
same as it had been for several 
years. It was not by accident that 
we called it the Canadian Camping 
“bulletin”. One could not call a 
mimeographed affair a magazine. 

The first real Canadian Camping 
“magazine” was published in Feb¬ 
ruary of 1949 when for the first 
time it appeared in print. 

Again, owing to lack of funds, 
this important development would 
not have been possible had not Mr. 
Fred Haiblen of Toronto stepped 
in and assumed the financial re¬ 
sponsibility for what at best was a 
risky venture. Miss Mary Edgar 
gave continuity to the magazine by 
acting as its editor for five more 
years and was succeeded by Mrs. 
G. W. Flynn. 

Miss Dais L. Gass, president of 
the C.C.A. in 1946 aptly expressed 
the hopes of the Association when 
she said in the leading editorial of 
the first edition of Canadian Camp¬ 
ing: - 

“Now it starts in its humble way 
— may it grow like the acorn and 
the oak, but most of all may it 
prove a tie between all of us in 
Canada. We can learn much from 
each other. May Canadian Camp¬ 
ing weave a bond of understanding, 
of mutual helpfulness and good 
will from sea to sea, and from the 
rivers to the end of the earth.” 

Many of you are more aware 
than 1 am of recent developments. 
To the Publications Committee 
under the Chairmanship of Don 
Groff we express our deep appre¬ 
ciation. 

To Ann Prewitt, who has as¬ 
sumed the responsibility for both 
editing and publishing our maga¬ 
zine, we wish the very best. 


16 


The Society Of Camp Directors 
Professional Directors Of Childrens’ Camps 

by Clifford Labbett, 

Director Camp Oconto, 

President, Society of Camp Directors 


Indeed an impressive title! And 
it is the intention of the people 
who compose this group of dedi¬ 
cated men and women to make the 
Society just that! While very young 
in terms of years, already this or¬ 
ganization has made its presence 
felt in the field of organized chil¬ 
drens' camping. Home is in To¬ 
ronto hut members are from both 
Canada and U.S.A. with the com¬ 
mon bond of camping. Founded in 
1969 with fifty-seven members at¬ 
tending the Inaugural Dinner held 
at the Rosedale Golf & Country 
Club, Toronto, on May 12, 1969, 
its membership has increased and 
attendance at the twice yearly meet¬ 
ings has been good. 

The Society is the brain child of 
Dr. Harry Ebbs of Taylor Statten 
Camps. The first seeds were planted 
when Dr. Ebbs sent out a question¬ 
naire to the members of the On¬ 
tario Camping Association in 1968 
asking various questions about the 
interests and desires of childrens' 
camp directors and then reported 
back to the membership at the an¬ 
nual spring conference of the On¬ 
tario Camping Association in 1968. 
The next fall and winter several 
organizational meetings were held 
of those who had expressed an in¬ 
terest in forming an organization 
composed chiefly of camp directors. 
From these meetings came a name, 
a pro-tem constitution, a very 
strong desire to push ahead in this 
new field convinced that it would 
do much to raise and maintain high 
standards in the quality of those 
directing childrens' camps. The 
purpose of the Society is stated as 
being to establish and maintain 
professional practices in the direct¬ 
ing of childrens' camps and to en¬ 
sure qualified directorship in such 
camps. A board of five directors 
runs the affairs of the Society with 
each member serving a three year 
term. A president and other officers 
are elected from this board by the 


board. Membership is composed of 
three classes — “Fellows", those ac¬ 
tively or previously engaged in the 
profession of camping in a senior 
capacity and those actively engaged 
in an allied discipline with a pro¬ 
fessional relationship to camping. 
“Honorary Fellows", those who 
have made outstanding contribu¬ 
tions in the fields of camping and 
allied fields. “Emeritus Fellozus", 
those who are retired from active 
participation in camping because of 
age, health or long service. At the 
inaugural dinner the following 
zuere unanimously elected as Hon¬ 
orary Fellows — Miss Mary Edgar, 
Miss Ferna Haiti day, Miss Mary 
Hamilton, Mr. Charles Plewman, 
Mrs. Taylor Statten. 

While in some respects this nezu 
organization is similar to existing 
camping associations across the 
country it was felt that membership 
should be restricted to those ac¬ 
tively directing a camp or who hold 
a senior position in a camp, per¬ 
sons retired from camping but still 
very interested and those active in 
an allied field. In this to ay much 
of the necessary and desirable busi¬ 
ness of a camping association could 
be done away with and projects 
undertaken that were of more pro¬ 
fessional interest, such as papers on 
camping subjects and research into 
some of the many facets of chil¬ 
drens' camping. 

Following the inaugural dinner 
nominations for directors were re¬ 
ceived and elections held. Dr. Harry 
Ebbs, Mr. Ron Johnstone, Mr. Clif¬ 
ford Labbett, Dr. Bruno Morawetz 
and Dr. Elsie Palter were elected to 
the Board. This group then elected 
Dr. Ebbs as the Society's first Presi¬ 
den t. 

Two yneetings are held each year 
— the second Thursday in Novem¬ 
ber and April — ivith the April 
meeting being the Annual Meeting 
and election of new directors. Dur¬ 


ing the interim the directors meet 
several times to look after the busi¬ 
ness of the Society and plan the 
semi-annual meetings. To date four 
of these meetings have been held 
and at them papers on various sub¬ 
jects have been presented by the fol¬ 
lowing — Donald Groff, Joseph 
Kronick, Dr. B. Morawetz, Dr. 
Mary Northxuay, David Palter, Jack 
Pearce, Elizabeth Raymer, Stanley 
Wild, and Kirk Wipper. Many of 
these papers have been reproduced 
in Canadian Caznping and Ameri¬ 
can publications. 

The Society is currently offering 
a $500 Research Fund to any un¬ 
dergraduate at a College or Uni¬ 
versity that zuishes to do research 
on some aspect of childrens' camp¬ 
ing. It is also working zuith the On¬ 
tario Camping Association on a 
joint proposal to have stricter li¬ 
censing of childrens' camps in On¬ 
tario and to have the O.C.A. made 
the governing body in Ontario. 
While this is Ontario business the 
majority of the Society's Fellozus 
are residents of Ontario — actively 
engaged in camping in Ontario — 
and any information and experi¬ 
ence gained here would enable both 
the Society and the O.C.A. to assist 
any other organization in a similar 
venture. 

Interest by camping people in 
other sections of Canada has been 
expressed and the Society welcomes 
questions concerning membership 
and the possibility of establishing 
sections or bra?zches in other parts 
of the country. Persons seeking 
membership are to be nominated 
by tzuo Fellozus and complete an 
application form. The annual fee 
is $25 which covers tzuo dinner 
meetings each year and copies of 
the papers given at Society meet¬ 
ings. Anyone zuishing information 
should contact the secretary — Mr. 
David Palter, 80 Old Colony Rd,. 
Willozudale, Ont.

II doit eviter egalement d’humilier

Un moniteur incoherent est un

d’ecoute et d’animation. 

Relations personnclles avec 
le campeur 

Jusqu’ici les relations du moni¬ 
teur sont purement techniques en 
vertu d’une autorite nccessaire im- 
posee par sa fonction. L’humanite 
de ses rapports n'en n’est pas 
moins pour cela ignoree, ceux-ci 
n ’etant pas a Fabri de toute impul¬ 
sion affective. Rien n’est plus im- 
previsible que le sentiment. Des 
liens s’etablissent naturellement 
avec plus ou moins d’intensite. 
Legality des sentiments est une 
chose tellement fragile, voire diffi¬ 
cile; la sympathie etant une capa¬ 
cite d’aflection revele par certaines 
affinites naturelles. Nous parlons 
alors de relations personnclles oil 
l’affectivite en regie Fin tensile. 
Tout ceci impose discretion, deli- 
catcsse, comprehension et connais- 
sance de Fhumain. 

S’il est un domaine qui ne se 
commandc pas, e’est bien celui du 
sentiment. II est done important 
d’admettre que l’esprit de justice 
demeure un exigence primordiale 
pour le moniteur. Tout comporte- 
ment selectif, meme involontaire, 
presente un handicap pour les re¬ 
lations humaines a l’interieur d’un 
groupe. La segregation reside sou- 
vent dans la tete du moniteur. 
L’equilibre est difficile mais qu’est- 
ce que le juste milieu? D’abord 
justice ne vent pas dire “rasage” 
(tout le monde au meme niveau). 
Je crois que ce serait une erreur 
fondamentale. Personne n’a les 
memes problemes, et par conse- 
cjiient, les solutions doivent varier 
pour chacun. “Chaque campeur a 
un droit strict d’etre eduque pour 
lui-meme’’. Chacjue rencontre avec 
un campeur doit etre personnelle 
et humanisante. 

II ne s’agit pas d’aimer moins ou 
plus tel ou tel campeur. II s’agit de 
percevoir le campeur comme une 
entile a respecter dans ses fibres les 


plus profondes. Les exigences de 
telles relations ne relevent pas 
d’une simple sympathie ou d’un 
sentiment de pi tie a l'egard d’un 
campeur ou d’un autre. C’est ici 
une question de responsabilite et 
de maturity. On admettra que le 
moniteur ne peut donner le change 
de ses faiblesses. Sa fonction com- 
mande une attitude consciente qui 
se soit pas livree au hasard. Le 
moniteur constitute pour le cam¬ 
peur un modele possible d’oii l'im- 
portance de sa valeur en tant que 
personne humaine. II suscitera ainsi 
le respect et la confiance. Puis en 
etant lui-meme, il y a de fortes 
chances que les campeurs soient 
eux-memes avec lui. 

Dans ses relations personnelles 
avec les campeurs le moniteur doit 
eviter de rechercher ses propres 
interets. C’est deja se rechercher 
que s’attendre a certaines consola¬ 
tions, si legitimes soient-elles. La 
reconnaissance est un sentiment 
d’adulte et l’enfant n’est pas tou- 
jours responsable de ses affections. 
De la l’attitude ambivalente (posi¬ 
tive et negative) qu’engendrent 
certaines relations dites affcctives, 
voire sentimentales. On espere en 
vain si l’on se recherche; il ne faut 
pas confondre sentimentalite avec 
affection. Plusieurs jeunes moni- 
teurs se font jouer des tours avec 
leurs sentiments. On n’aide pas les 
autrcs pour attendre d’eux un re¬ 
tour, une reconnaissance de ses 
actes. Un ami-professeur m’ecrivait 
ceci que je trouve fort a propos: 
“Il n’y a pas de plus riche amour 
que la depossession. Etre capable de 
se ‘deposseder’ de quelqu’un, c’est 
l’affirmer et faire etre, venir au 
monde. Ce sont mes eleves et non 
pas hues’ eleves ‘a moi’. I Is s’appar- 
tiennent. I Is doivent s'affirmer selon 
leur loi propre. Si je puis les aider 
(et je le puis) je le fais. Je marche 
un bout de route avec eux. Au bout 
de cette route, ils prendront la leur 
. . . Saint! S’ils m’invitent a nou¬ 
veau, j’y serai. Je ne les aime pas 
pour le merite que j’en aurai, il est 
consequent. Je les aime pour ce 
qu’ils sont et ce qu’ils sont appel^s 
a devenir.’’ Voila pourquoi le moni¬ 
teur doit mobiliser des quality 
d’evcilleur cFhonnncs et de presence 
humaine equilibree. 

L’authenticite de notre affection 
se mesure a la quality de notre don. 
Voir dans celui du campeur sa 
capacite d’amour cventuellement 
muri et equilibre, e'est rencontrer 
ce qu’il y a de plus fondamentale- 
ment humain en lui. L’affection 
vraie requiert de l’effacement. Elle 
n’implique pas pour la prolonger 
une presence permanente. L’equi- 


libre affectif du moniteur doit 
devenir un gage de maturite et de 
stability dans ses relations person¬ 
nelles. Celles-ci doivent s’etablir 
d’humain a humain avec tous les 
imponderables impliques. Il im- 
porte surement de prendre au 
serieux les sentiments du campeur 
car ils le sont vraiment. Pour cer¬ 
tains, l’affection manifestee est a la 
source d’un geste, d’une parole; 
pour d’autres des rapports entrenus 
iavorisent l’eclosion d’un senti¬ 
ment, et la securite s’y melant, ils 
se dccouvrent une sympathie nou- 
velle pour leur moniteur. Le cam¬ 
peur a besoin que la tendresse lui 
soit revelee. Le moniteur a fonction 
de relations humaines et s’y sous- 
traire marquerait un point negatif 
au tableau de ses responsabilites a 
assumer. 

Pour des relations humaines vraies 

Normalement le campeur a des 
relations naturelles avec ses moni- 
teurs. Le camp ne favorise pas les 
prejuges. Le campeur sait quelle 
sympathie ses moniteurs lui te- 
moigneront. Ses relations avec eux 
sont pour lui une source de vigueur 
et de confiance qui se transmettent 
au niveau de ses relations avec ses 
copains. C’est un ordre naturel (de 
dependance a Findependance) que 
le moniteur doit favoriser. 

Le campeur a besoin d’appui et 
pour lui le moniteur devient un 
point de repere ou ses yeux sont 
fixes. Parler d’education, c’est cher- 
cher le lieu vital du campeur dans 
un reseau d’interrelations qui le 
mettent en situation d’experience 
de vie. De la l’importance de l’ac- 
cueil, de la comprehension et de 
l’engagement k realiser. Le moni¬ 
teur doit etre pleinement conscient 
de sa relation avec le campeur. 
Si non il le domestiquera, le domi- 
nera. Ce sera une education de 
“vase a remplir” qui ne respectera 
pas l’ordre naturel des relations. Le 
moniteur deshumanisera ainsi sa 
relation. Que de ravages irrepa- 
rables ignores. 

Nous le savons, les schemes tra- 
ditionnels sont de moins en moins 
determinants dans le comporte- 
ment vecu des campeurs. Voila 
pourquoi parler de relations hu¬ 
maines, c’est d’abord insister sur 
toute la dynamique du comporte- 
ment vecu. Echanger avec autrui 
exige, qu’implicitement, il y ait eu 
echange avec soi-meme. Le dia¬ 
logue n’est pas une relation livree 
au hasard. Il faut justement eviter 
tout acte qui empeche de “prendre 
conscience’’. Tout cela s’evalue en 
tenues d’authenticite, e’est-a-dire

Continued from page 9 

authority is obvious, the more im¬ 
portant and repeated the overt 
signs become. The counsellor 
should be capable of prevention, 
organization and firmness. A pun¬ 
ishment that has to be administered 
will not be collective or corporal. 
His indulgence should be without 
weakness. The counsellor is prim¬ 
arily an enabler, not a trainer. He 
also should avoid humiliating a 
camper in public. In this aspect, 
the counsellor deals, in a deep sense, 
with the personal dignity of the 
camper. An incoherent counsellor 
is a weak one. Any tyrannical dis¬ 
cipline will destroy his relations 
with the camper and even with the 
group. The counsellor should com¬ 
promise with all situations that 
arise between him and his group, 
and always keep in mind that his 
function is limited to listening and 
animating. 

Personal Relations with the 
Camper 

Until now, the relationships of 
the staff member have been tech¬ 
niques by virtue of an authority 
imposed by his job. The kindness 
of his relations, unsheltered from 
emotional impulses, are not in the 
least ignored. Nothing is more un¬ 
foreseeable than feelings. Ties are 
naturally created with more or less 
intensity. Equality in feelings is so 
fragile and difficult, sympathy being 
a capacity of affection revealed by 
some natural affinities. We are 
therefore talking about personal 
relations where the intensity of the 
feeling is controlled by the degree 
of affectivity. All of this demands 
discretion, scrupulousness, compre¬ 
hension and an understanding of 
the human being. 

Personal feelings cannot be con¬ 
trolled. It is therefore important to 
know that for the counsellor, jus¬ 
tice stays a prime requirement. All 
discriminatory behavior, even if 
involuntary, is a handicap for 
human relations inside a group. 
Segregation is often in the counsel¬ 
lor's mind. Social justice is difficult 
to obtain, but where is the middle 
road? First, justice does not mean 
“scraping" (everybody at the same 
level). I think that would be a 
basic mistake. Nobody has the same 
problems and, therefore, the solu¬ 
tions must vary for everybody. 
“Each camper has the specific right 
to be educated for himself." Each 
acquaintance with the camper must 
be personal and humanizing. It is 
not a question of loving one camper 
more than another one. It is to see 
him as an entity to be respected in 


its deepest senses. The require¬ 
ments of such relations towards the 
camper do not come from a simple 
feeling of sympathy or pity for one 
or the other. It is a question of 
responsibility and maturity. We 
will admit that the Counsellor can¬ 
not mislead others as to his weak¬ 
nesses. His function demands a 
conscious attitude that should not 
be left to chance. For the camper, 
the counsellor represents a possible 
example as far as the importance of 
human value is concerned. He will 
inspire, in this way, respect and 
confidence. Furthermore, by being 
himself, there are good chances for 
the campers to be themselves with 
him. 

In his personal relations with the 
camper, the counsellor should avoid 
acting in his own interests. Yet he 
does so if he expects certain re¬ 
wards, even if they are justifiable. 
Gratitude is an adult feeling and 
the child is not always accountable 
for his affections. 

From this point on, comes the 
ambivalent attitude (positive and 
negative) that certain affective and 
sentimental relationships encour¬ 
age. We hope in vain if we are 
working towards our own interests; 
we should not mistake sentimental¬ 
ity for affection. A lot of young 
counsellors are being tricked by 
their feelings. We do not help 
others if we look for their gratitude 
in return. A professor, a good 
friend of mine, once wrote some¬ 
thing to me that I found well to the 
point: “There is no greater love 
than the one of dispossession. To be 
capable of ‘dispossessing’ ourselves 
of somebody is to assert him and to 
make him exist, come to life. They 
are my students and not ‘my own 
students’. They belong to them¬ 
selves. They should assert them¬ 
selves according to their own laws. 
If I can help them (and I can) I 
will do it. I walk part of the way 
with them. At the end of this road, 
they will take their own . . . Sal¬ 
vation! If they invite me again, I 
will be there. I do not like them for 
the glory I will get from them, it is 
rational. I like them for what they 
are and what they will be." It is the 
reason why the counsellor has to 
put in action “mind awakener" 
qualities and a well balanced per¬ 
sonality. 

The authenticity of our affection 
is measured by the quality of what 
we give. To see in the camper’s gift 
his capacity of a well balanced and 
possibly matured love, is to per¬ 
ceive what is most fundamentally 
human in him. True affection re¬ 
quires self-effacement. A pennanent 


presence is not necessary to prolong 
it. The effective balance of the 
counsellor should become a mea¬ 
sure of maturity and stability in his 
personal relations. These relations 
should be established from person 
to person, with all the implications 
of the intangible factors. It is surely 
important to take the campers’ feel¬ 
ings seriously, because they really 
are. For some, the affection is man¬ 
ifested by a word, a gesture; for 
others, continuous relations are 
favourable to the development of a 
feeling, and with security being in¬ 
volved, they will discover a new 
sympathy for their counsellors. The 
camper needs tenderness to be re¬ 
vealed to him. Human relations is 
the counsellor’s duty and to neglect 
it would be a negative point in the 
overall responsibilities he assumes. 
For True Human Relations 

The camper normally has nat¬ 
ural human relations with his coun¬ 
sellors. The camp does not favour 
prejudices. The camper knows what 
kind of sympathy his counsellors 
show towards him. His relations 
with them are for him a source of 
vigour and confidence that is trans¬ 
mitted at the level of his relations 
with his companions. The counsel¬ 
lor has to encourage a natural order 
(of dependence and independence). 
The camper needs support and the 
counsellor becomes the landmark 
on whom his eyes are fixed. To talk 
of education is to search for the 
place vital to the camper in a net¬ 
work of interrelationships which 
puts him in the situation of life 
experience. From this point the 
importance of reception, of com¬ 
prehension and of engagement can 
be realized. The counsellor should 
be fully conscious of his relation 
with the camper. Otherwise he will 
domesticate and dominate him. It 
will be an education of “filling up 
an empty vase" which will not re¬ 
spect the natural order of relations. 
The counsellor will this way de¬ 
humanize his relationship. What 
ravages; irretrievable and ignored! 

We know that traditional schemes 
are less and less determinative in 
the behaviour of campers. When 
we speak of human relations, it is 
first of all to insist on the dynamics 
of usual behavior. To share with 
others demands that, implicitly, 
there had been a sharing with one¬ 
self. Dialogue is not a relation left 
to chance. We have to avoid all 
action that prevents an “awakening 
to consciousness." All this is eval¬ 
uated in terms of authenticity, that 
is to say, TO BE TRUE. 

translated by the Canadian 
Amateur Sports Federation

Letters to the Editor 

Letters to the Editor are welcome and encouraged. It is hoped that this 
column will become a forum for a free discussion of ideas related to 
camping. All letters are subject to condensation. 


Dear Editor, 

I have just read and re-read Ed La 
Pierre's article on Youth Culture and 
Camping which appeared in the last 
edition oj Canadian Camping. 1 have 
done my best to let its contents sink in 
and have come away with the following 
impressions. 

First, the writer appears to be some¬ 
what belligerent and evidently is an¬ 
other one of the angry young men who 
thinks all people over 35 should be 
cremated. Maybe he comes from a fam¬ 
ily that has had a real generation gap; 
if so, I would like to remind him that 
there are many closely knit families 
which have never experienced a gen¬ 
eration gap that has resulted in hostility 
and loss of respect, even though its mem¬ 
bers are now 21 and 24 years of age. 
To be sure, they have held different 
outlooks and different ways of doing 
things but never with open hostility. 
With them sharing and dialogue has 
been the order of the day. 

Second. Apparently the adult is the 
big bad wolf. He is the one that makes 
all of the mistakes. In his open state¬ 
ment and I quote “the contents are for 
camp directors, administrators and lead¬ 
ers — these then, are the only people 
to be admonished. Nothing needs saying 
about the younger generation for with 
them everything is hunky dory. 

Third. Adults have made such a hash 
of camping that the “whole shebang" 
should he turned over to the youngsters 
to run. He says, and I quote, “Resident 
camps should be controlled by the 
campers themselves *. 

I am xvilling to concede that adults 
should have done a better job in shar¬ 
ing luith the campers on the decision 
making level, but to say that we should 
abdicate and turn everything over to in¬ 
experienced youngsters to run is sheer 
unadulterated nonsense. The prograxn 
and the ongoing life of camp should be 
the results of txvo age groups sharing 
and not of any one age group domin¬ 
ating. To turn everything over to the 
campers is simply to substitute one set 
of evils for the other. 

Can anyone imagine the increase that 
would take place in the number of 
campers injured, the number sick in the 
infirmary and the loss of life by drozvti- 
ing that xvould ensue if childern with 


their limited experience were in control. 

Fourth. Camp Directors, he infers, are 
all wrong in feeling that parents have 
vested them with authority. The young¬ 
sters should be alloxvcd to do xvhatever 
they like — / wonder! I xoonder hoxv 
many honest to goodness parents would 
send their ten-year-old boy to a camp 
xohere the Director made it clear that 
he would not in the final analysis exer¬ 
cise his best judgment and authority. 

To quote Ed, he says, “Most camp 
Administrators and supervisors look up¬ 
on their authority as replacing that of 
the parent". What is wrong xoith that? 
I xvould say that it is to the credit of 
Camp Directors that they have person¬ 
ally felt a real responsibility for every¬ 
thing that had to do xvith the xvelfare 
and happiness of those entrusted to 
their care. Organized camping has flour¬ 
ished in Canada because of the confi¬ 
dence that parents have come to feel 
about those xvho operate them. 

Fifth. It seems to me that Ed has 
mixed his drinks. A good deal of xvhat 
he says xvould have some application to 
youth of from 17 on, but xalien he ap¬ 
plies the same philosophy to an age 
group of 7 to 16 he just misses the boat. 
What have the communes he refers to 
got to do xvith this age group. 

Sixth. Camps he says are turning kids 
off. I have just passed through a camp 
of 2oo boys. 1 don't know where you 
could find a happier gang of kids. I 
may be xvrong, but I xvould say that 
camps are just as popular as ever with 
the 8 to 14 year olds and as for those 
older, it never has had too great an 
appeal. 

Seventh. Apparently Ed xvants more 
permissiveness in sex, drugs, and indi¬ 
vidual liberties. He states and I quote 
“Most Directors know only the negative 
side of the “Drug Culture" (the italics 
are mine) “Sex is worried about, “con¬ 
trol" he says “is assured by authority". 

What, speaking positively, does Ed 
want? Free love! Drug usage! License! 

His real liang-up however seems to 
be authority. I have nexvs for Ed and 
that is where there is no authority you 
have anarchy, — xvhere the individual 
does xvhatever he likes you have chaos. 
Can Ed mention any area of life hi 
which it isn't necessary to use authority 
in order to maintain order. If he doubts 


this, let him remove the police from 
any city for two xveeks and he xvill get 
his ansxver in big capital letters. 

In conclusion. Sure we older folks 
have made our full share of mistakes. 
Even at that, xve have probably made 
more progress than any other genera¬ 
tion. True, we didn't have all the an¬ 
swers, but neither xvill Ed's generation, 
and what is more, they will make their 
mistakes too. 

If camping is to get the best results, 
all of us, both young and old xvill have 
to xvork and share together and respect 
each others views. 

Personally, I have to admit that 1 
believe that a good group of 35-year- 
olds, if sitting in the seats of the inighty, 
xvould do a better job of solving the 
xvorld's problems than the present tired 
outfit schooled in the out moded prac¬ 
tices of the past, but that's an entirely 
different story. 

C. F. Plexvman

Dear L.D. 

Mr. L. Douglas Campbell of Calgary, 
the originator of and prime moving 
force behind the idea of a national 
trail, is compiling a list of names and 
addresses of interested persons. Much 
help is needed in studying and planning 
the immense scheme and Camping As¬ 
sociation members across the country 
are invited to lend assistance. 

Anyone interested should communi¬ 
cate directly with L. D. Campbell, Na¬ 
tional Trail, c/o Box 6623 — Station 
D, Calgary 2, Alberta.

BOOKS FOR CAMP 

TOM TICHENOR'S PUPPETS 
by To?7i TicheTior. (Abingdo7i Press) 
G. R. Welch Company, Limited, 
222 Eva7is Avenue, Toronto 18, 
Ontario —§6. 25 

Tom Tichenor, the noted pup¬ 
peteer, says that “a puppet must 
live”. The little animal or charac¬ 
ter that you have created must 
come alive from your fingers and 
heart. 

Tichenor's book lives and is ani¬ 
mated throughout in the same 
imaginative way. He introduces his 
own puppets to the reader one at a 
time and soon Poindexter, Witchie, 
Marco Polo Bear, Ex Libris the 
Bookworm, and all the others be¬ 
come very real. 

There are patetrns and directions 
how to make puppets from the 
simplest hand puppet (made from 
a stretch sock) to a complicated 
elaborate marionette. 

Seven complete plays are in¬ 
cluded. There are photographs and 
instructions for making a puppet 
playhouse and other directions for 
staging. 

Everything is included in this 
book that would be needed to en¬ 
hance any arts and crafts program 
at a camp. It will stimulate the 
creativity of your campers and pro¬ 
vide humorous entertainment for 
all. 


FOLLOW THE BUTTERFLY 
STREAM by Lore7\z Boyd. (Abing¬ 
don Press) G. R. Welch Company, 
Limited, 222 Evans Avenue, Tor- 
07ito 18, 07itario.— $3.75 

Lorenz Boyd captures his reader 
with an enchanting approach to a 
nature book on butterflies. The 
reader is led through the forest and 
beside streams as he follows the 
butterfly through its life cycle. 

Did you know that butterflies 
taste with their feet? Did you know 
that dragonflies rest with their 
wings spread while damselflies rest 
with their wings closed? 

The photographs are worth spe¬ 
cial mention because they are 
charming as well as of extraordin¬ 
ary quality. This beautiful little 
book is an introduction to butter¬ 
flies and should be in every camp 
library.

NOW AVAILABLE 

The Centenary Journey Commit¬ 
tee of the Canadian Camping As¬ 
sociation is pleased to announce 
that the “Journal” which tells the 
story of the project is now avail¬ 
able. It includes “their story” which 
relates the historical significance of 
each segment of the journey and 
“our story” of the experiences of 
Young Canadians in 1967. Maps 
are provided to show the route 
taken in Canada’s hundredth birth¬ 
day. The publication is available at 
the special price of $1.50 plus 25c 
for mailing and handling from the 
Canadian Camping Association, 
102 Eglinton St. East, Suite 203, 
Toronto, Ontario.

POST-CAMP 

by Jody Ashenhurst 
Camp Northway Lodge 


Sunset is at hand, and Northway sleeps in peace. 

Gone are the canoes — they are packed like 
sardines into boarded cabins. 

Gone are the docks — they are huddled together 
in the bay, grimly awaiting the wind and snow. 

Gone are the sailboats — dismembered beyond 
recognition, their parts are stored fondly away. 

Weathered logs and rotten boards melt into the 
surrounding woods, 

Lacking the roofs of canvas that used to dance so 
merrily along the shore. 


And so the woods, with open arms, reach out to 
reclaim our summer home. 

For one day (that dreaded day when the agonies 
of parting hung limp in the air) 

The sun frolicked with the leaves, creating those 
glorious but painful greens and golds that only 
come at sunset 

And then the sky was overcast — the evening had 
set in: 

The skeleton of summer now holds only ghosts and 
fading echoes of laughter. 


Then the night. 

But during the night, which seems so black and 
long, 

A fire burns — a glow which is the strength that 
comes from having known peace of mind. 

The courage to face the endless midnight which 
wreaks havoc on our sense of justice and 
fellowship — 

We face the winter and our city-selves with 
renewed confidence 

Because we have known Northway. 


And then, inevitably. 
Comes the dawn.
